explain.say: A muscle is made of long cells called muscle fibres, packed with protein threads that pull. When you make muscles work hard, they adapt so the same work feels easier next time.

faq.a: Muscles grow mainly because each fibre gets thicker, packed with more protein threads, rather than by making lots of new fibres. This happens after repeated hard work and recovery.
asks: Do we get new muscle fibres?

faq.q: Why do muscles ache the day after exercise?
faq.a: Unusual or hard exercise causes tiny strains in muscle fibres, and the repair process brings swelling and soreness a day or two later. It is not caused by lactic acid, which clears within an hour or so.
Satellite cells are muscle stem cells that sit along the outside of muscle fibres. After hard work or injury they divide and fuse with the fibres, helping repair and enlarge them.

faq.q: Why do people get stronger before their muscles get bigger?
faq.a: In the first weeks, the nervous system learns to activate more muscle fibres together and coordinate them better. Muscle size catches up later.
asks: How do nerves make you stronger?
Why does strength come before size?

faq.q: What happens to muscles that are not used?
faq.a: If muscles are not used, for example when a leg is in a cast, the fibres break down protein and shrink. This is called atrophy, and the muscle can rebuild when used again.
asks: Why do muscles shrink in a cast?

facts: Muscle growth comes mainly from existing fibres getting thicker, called hypertrophy.
Satellite cells are stem cells that help repair and grow skeletal muscle.

quiz.say: In the first couple of weeks of training, where does most of the extra strength come from?
quiz.show: Early strength gains come mostly from…

options.show: Nerves switching on more fibres together
options.say: Nerves switching on more fibres together

quiz.why: The nervous system learns to recruit and coordinate more muscle fibres before muscles grow much.

wrong.2: Blood flow rises during exercise, but it does not explain lasting strength gains.
